html:
From the diamond rush at Kimberley in the 1870s onward, Basotho men left their mountain country in great numbers to work in South African mines, and mine wages became the main income of Lesotho for a century.

At its height, in the 1970s and 1980s, over a hundred thousand Basotho men worked on the gold mines of the Witwatersrand, often for most of their working lives, coming home once a year. Their earnings paid for cattle, school fees and weddings, while women ran the farms and households.

Basotho miners were known for shaft-sinking work, and migrants created famo, an accordion music of the road and the mines. When the mines cut jobs from the 1990s, Lesotho lost its main source of income, and turned to textiles and to selling water to South Africa.
sum: From the diamond rush at Kimberley in the 1870s onward, Basotho men left their mountain country in great numbers to work in South African mines, and mine wages became the main income of Lesotho for a century.
